title: Job exposure: Which tasks vanish changes outcomes
desc: Distinguishes task automation from occupational disappearance and shows aggregate resilience can conceal redistribution within and between firms.

kps.k: Task automation measures exposure, not the disappearance of whole jobs.
kps.d: The cluster’s central proposition is that employment depends on what follows task substitution: lower prices can expand demand, workers can shift effort, firms can redesign jobs, and innovation can create new work. Frey and Osborne classify about 47% of US employment in the 2010 job mix as highly susceptible to computerisation, but explicitly do not forecast actual job losses. The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market likewise shows that net occupational demand remains theoretically ambiguous without restrictive assumptions about substitution elasticities; its patent measure captures capabilities targeted by innovation, not demonstrated displacement.

qs.q: We make no attempt to estimate the number of jobs that will actually be automated, and focus on potential job automatability over some unspecified number of years.
qs.a: The Future of Employment: How Susceptible Are Jobs to Computerisation? · Academia · 2017

qs.q: This means that without strong restrictions on the values of the various elasticity of substitution parameters, it is impossible to sign the net impacts of task-level substitution on the demand for occupations.
qs.a: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market · Academia · 2020

kps.k: The debate moves beyond routine-task intensity without discarding task-based analysis.
kps.d: Autor, Levy and Murnane link US computerisation during 1960–1998 to declining routine labour input and rising nonroutine cognitive input, largely within industries. Their framework concerns tasks programmable at the time, not permanent limits on machines. Frey and Osborne argue that pattern recognition extends substitution into nonroutine work, leaving engineering bottlenecks such as creative and social intelligence. Bessen challenges routine intensity as a sufficient explanation of adoption: occupational payoffs, wages and existing skills also matter. These positions differ over technological boundaries and adoption incentives rather than whether tasks matter.

qs.q: We argue that computer capital (1) substitutes for workers in performing cognitive and manual tasks that can be accomplished by following explicit rules; and (2) complements workers in performing nonroutine problem- solving and complex communications tasks.
qs.a: The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Exploration · Academia · 2003

qs.q: This is be- cause recent developments in ML and MR, building upon big data, allow for pattern recognition, and thus enable computer capital to rapidly substitute for labour across a wide range of non-routine tasks.
qs.a: The Future of Employment: How Susceptible Are Jobs to Computerisation? · Academia · 2017

kps.k: Historical employment resilience does not establish that productivity gains will reliably protect labour.
kps.d: Bessen associates computer use with roughly 0.9% additional annual employment growth in adopting occupations during 1980–2013, offset by inter-occupation substitution to an estimated net contribution of −0.07% annually. Acemoglu and Restrepo’s 2019 postwar decomposition instead emphasises stronger displacement, weaker creation of labour-intensive tasks and slower productivity growth in recent decades. These findings use different outcomes and scopes: Bessen models occupational employment effects within industries, while Acemoglu and Restrepo analyse the economy-wide wage bill and labour shares. Their framework distinguishes productivity-driven demand expansion from reinstatement through genuinely new tasks in which labour has comparative advantage.

qs.q: Overall, inter-occupation substitution offsets the growth effect so that     the net effect of computer use on total employment is negligible (-.07% per year).
qs.a: How Computer Automation Affects Occupations: Technology, Jobs, and Skills · Academia · 2015

qs.q: Our empirical decomposition suggests that the slower growth of employment over the last three decades is accounted for by an acceleration in the displacement effect, especially in manufacturing, a weaker reinstatement effect, and slower growth of productivity than in previous decades.
qs.a: Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor · Academia · 2019

kps.k: Which tasks disappear can matter as much as how many disappear.
kps.d: Autor and Thompson’s Expertise framework distinguishes automating supporting tasks, which can raise incumbents’ productivity and wages, from automating expert tasks, which can broaden entry and reduce the scarcity value of expertise. They report contrasting relative wage and employment changes for accounting and inventory clerks during 1980–2018, and independent wage associations for task quantities and expertise changes. This complements, rather than replaces, demand-based explanations. Bessen identifies another distributional mechanism: costly occupation-specific learning can widen wage gaps within occupations even without substantial aggregate job loss. Expertise acknowledges demand saturation as an alternative explanation and calls its evidence illustrative rather than definitive.

qs.q: Specifically, the model predicts that changing expertise requirements have countervailing effects on wages and employment: automation that decreases expertise requirements reduces wages but permits the entry of less expert workers; automation that raises requirements raises wages but reduces the set of qualified workers.
qs.a: Expertise · Academia · 2025

qs.q: The model contemplates a different sort of skill-biased technical change, one where the relevant skills are occupation- specific rather than corresponding to schooling per se.15 Moreover, to the extent that new occupation-specific skills are costly to acquire, the model implies that wage inequality may increase within occupations.
qs.a: How Computer Automation Affects Occupations: Technology, Jobs, and Skills · Academia · 2015

kps.k: AI can redistribute employment within and between firms while leaving aggregate effects difficult to detect.
kps.d: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market models how uneven task improvements let workers reallocate effort toward less affected activities. It reports that AI exposure accounts for about 14% of variation in occupational employment-share growth, split roughly equally between within-firm reallocation and differences in employers’ AI use; the supplied excerpt does not give sample dates. It also reports employment-share declines approaching 2% over five years in business, financial and engineering occupations—not absolute job-loss estimates. Indirect effects matter: workers with little direct exposure can lose employment share when their employers grow more slowly than AI adopters. Separately reported prior studies associate AI adoption with firm growth and AI exposure with reduced establishment hiring; these are different measures and outcomes, not a resolved contradiction.

qs.q: By contrast, when improvements are uneven—some tasks more affected than others—workers reallocate their effort toward the less                                                       19 ^Laffected task.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market · Academia · 2025

qs.q: They find that exposure is associated with lower hiring at the establishment level, but aggregate occupation/industry effects are too small to detect over that period.
qs.a: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from U.S. Résumé and Job Posting Data · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Legal work illustrates why task forecasts, occupational forecasts and observed employment must remain separate.
kps.d: Autor, Levy and Murnane place legal writing among tasks complemented by computers; Frey and Osborne later predict its automation while still classifying lawyers as low risk because of creative and social intelligence. Their model places paralegals and legal assistants at high risk. Bessen, meanwhile, reports 1.1% annual full-time-equivalent growth in legal support employment during 2000–2013 despite offshoring. Historical growth neither disproves future susceptibility nor guarantees resilience under generative AI. The supplied seniority-bias excerpt asks whether simpler junior tasks create disproportionate exposure within high-skill fields; it supplies no results establishing junior displacement.

qs.q: In the present study, we will argue that legal writing and truck driving will soon be automated, while persuading, for instance, will not.
qs.a: The Future of Employment: How Susceptible Are Jobs to Computerisation? · Academia · 2017

qs.q: 10 From 2000 through 2013, fulltime equivalent jobs for legal assistants, paralegals, and legal support  occupations grew 1.1% per year, faster than the workforce.
qs.a: How Computer Automation Affects Occupations: Technology, Jobs, and Skills · Academia · 2015

kps.k: Job redesign and worker adjustment make fixed occupational classifications incomplete guides to AI’s effects.
kps.d: Work at the Frontier argues that changing activity costs can produce either narrower specialist roles or broader generalist roles, changing the skills employers reward. It cites historical within-title task changes but notes that employment records capture them only after they become observable. Answering the Call of Automation leaves unresolved whether, when and how replacement work emerges. Its telephone-operator evidence finds no wage or employment-share spillovers in the substitute occupations examined, not a general absence of adjustment costs. Possible losses of workplace social ties and family effects remain research hypotheses.

qs.q: When automation changes the cost of performing particular activities, firms may split an existing job into narrower roles, allowing workers to specialize, or even recombine activities into a broader role, creating more generalists.
qs.a: Work at the Frontier: How AI is expanding what people do at work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: As a result, questions such as whether, when, and how new work will materialize to offset the jobs lost to automation are not fully resolved.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Practical responses should track changing work and skill demands, not infer staffing cuts directly from exposure scores.
kps.d: The synthesis implies assessing adoption incentives, demand responsiveness, remaining expertise, job redesign and new-task creation alongside technical capability. Bessen prioritises occupation-specific learning rather than simply increasing graduation rates; Frey and Osborne recommend creative and social skills; Acemoglu and Restrepo emphasise conditions that support labour-intensive innovation. None guarantees protection. The evidence also requires methodological restraint: historical computer-use studies face causal and measurement limits, occupational classifiers test susceptibility rather than realised losses, and residual task decompositions do not directly observe every displaced or newly created task. These sources provide mechanisms for analysing AI, not a settled forecast of legal employment.

qs.q: The challenge will not be met simply by increasing college graduation rates.
qs.a: How Computer Automation Affects Occupations: Technology, Jobs, and Skills · Academia · 2015

qs.q: For workers to win the race, however, they will have to acquire creative and social skills.
qs.a: The Future of Employment: How Susceptible Are Jobs to Computerisation? · Academia · 2017

vlens.an:
The selected academia and research sources collectively build on the proposition that task exposure is not equivalent to occupational disappearance. Their common reasoning is that net employment depends on mechanisms following substitution: demand expansion after cost reductions, worker reallocation toward less-affected tasks, job and task reorganisation, productivity effects, creation of new labour-intensive tasks, and differences in growth across firms. Several sources materially deepen the proposition by showing why the identity of removed tasks matters: automating supporting rather than expert tasks can change the scarcity of expertise, qualified labour supply, wages and employment in different directions. Recent AI research also adds evidence that aggregate stability can conceal within-firm reallocation and differences between employers.

There is material internal variation rather than a single forecast. Historical computerisation studies report ambiguous or near-zero net employment effects while finding substantial redistribution and skill or wage effects. Acemoglu and Restrepo are more cautious about extrapolating that resilience, arguing that stronger displacement and weaker creation of new tasks can suppress labour demand. Frey and Osborne adopt a broader view of technical susceptibility, extending exposure beyond routine work, but explicitly do not estimate realised job losses and omit productivity and within-occupation reallocation. The telephone-automation study leaves replacement work unresolved, while the seniority-focused GenAI excerpt poses junior exposure as a research question rather than reporting a result. Two bibliography-only excerpts provide no basis for determining a position. These differences concern mechanisms, scope, historical period and evidentiary strength; they do not amount to rejection of the cluster’s principal distinction. Because this is a curated set, the synthesis characterises only these sources and not academia or researchers generally.

qs.q: Comparing predicted to realized changes, we estimate that about 14% of the variation in occupational employment share growth can be attributed to their AI exposure during our sample period—roughly half from within-firm reallocation away from exposed tasks, and half from differences in average AI use across occupations’ employers.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Nevertheless, our expertise framework suggests a complementary but distinct conceptual focus for analyzing the relationship between automation and the value of labor: it is not merely                                                   52 ^Lthe quantity of tasks performed by an occupation or demographic group that determines demand for its labor, but also the scarcity of the expertise required to perform those tasks.
qs.a: Expertise · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied legal-tech-vendor source accepts the cluster’s principal distinction between automating tasks and eliminating occupations, but materially extends it by challenging fixed-task assumptions. Its central contribution is that changes in activity costs can prompt firms to redraw job boundaries—either splitting jobs into specialist roles or recombining activities into broader generalist roles—thereby changing both the work people perform and the skills rewarded. This strengthens the cluster’s emphasis on job redesign and explains why exposure scores based on current occupational bundles are incomplete guides to employment outcomes. The source does not predict one uniform direction of change: specialisation and generalisation are both possible. It also qualifies the historical evidence because changes become visible in job advertisements, titles and employment records only after redesign has occurred. As only one curated source is supplied for this professional voice, there is no basis for inferring wider vendor prevalence or cross-source variation.

qs.q: When automation changes the cost of performing particular activities, firms may split an existing job into narrower roles, allowing workers to specialize, or even recombine activities into a broader role, creating more generalists.
qs.a: Work at the Frontier: How AI is expanding what people do at work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: The key point is that the bundle of human work – and therefore the bundle of skills rewarded in the labor market – changes in response to AI.
qs.a: Work at the Frontier: How AI is expanding what people do at work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

elens.an: The pre-2015 foundation source supports the proposition by treating computerization as substitution for particular routine tasks and complementarity with nonroutine cognitive tasks, rather than as automatic occupational disappearance. Its evidence of substantial task reallocation within industries and nominally unchanged occupations reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on job redesign and redistribution beneath aggregate employment measures. It also explicitly finds industry employment-share effects ambiguous, because replacing human routine-task input with computers does not determine the resulting level of product demand or employment. Material internal qualifications concern scope and inference: the routine/nonroutine boundary reflects what was programmable at the time, not a permanent technological frontier; some predicted relationships, especially for routine manual tasks, were not observed; and the educational-demand estimates are illustrative and observational rather than experimental. These caveats limit causal and forward-looking claims but do not weaken the source’s overall support for the task-based proposition.

qs.q: We argue that computer capital (1) substitutes for workers in performing cognitive and manual tasks that can be accomplished by following explicit rules; and (2) complements workers in performing nonroutine problem- solving and complex communications tasks.
qs.a: The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Exploration · Academia · 2003

qs.q: By contrast, the predic- tion for the employment share of routine-task-intensive industries is ambiguous since these industries should have differentially substituted computer capital for labor input.
qs.a: The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Exploration · Academia · 2003

elens.an:
The 2015–2022 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core distinction between task-level automation exposure and occupational disappearance, while materially developing the mechanisms that determine employment outcomes. Common reasons include demand expansion after productivity-driven price reductions, substitution between occupations, workers’ reallocation toward remaining tasks, job reorganisation, and the creation of new labour-intensive tasks. They also show why aggregate resilience can conceal distributional effects across occupations, wage levels and workers with different capacities to acquire occupation-specific skills.

Material internal variation concerns the expected balance of these mechanisms. Frey and Osborne offer a forward-looking susceptibility classifier and argue that machine learning extends automation beyond routine work, but expressly do not estimate realised job losses and omit productivity and within-occupation reallocation effects. Bessen’s historical analysis finds growth in computer-using occupations largely offset by inter-occupation substitution, producing a near-zero estimated aggregate employment effect within its scope, while also identifying low-wage losses and increased within-occupation inequality. Acemoglu and Restrepo are less reassuring: their decomposition attributes recent labour-demand weakness to stronger displacement, weaker creation of new labour-intensive tasks and slower productivity growth. The patent-exposure study reinforces the theoretical ambiguity of net occupational demand and adds task creation and reorganisation as further channels. One supplied record contains only bibliography, so its position is indeterminate. These curated sources therefore do not establish a universal consensus or a settled forecast; they provide complementary models and evidence showing that outcomes depend on which tasks are automated and what demand, redesign and new-task effects follow.

qs.q: We make no attempt to estimate the number of jobs that will actually be automated, and focus on potential job automatability over some unspecified number of years.
qs.a: The Future of Employment: How Susceptible Are Jobs to Computerisation? · Academia · 2017

qs.q: Our empirical decomposition suggests that the slower growth of employment over the last three decades is accounted for by an acceleration in the displacement effect, especially in manufacturing, a weaker reinstatement effect, and slower growth of productivity than in previous decades.
qs.a: Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor · Academia · 2019

elens.an: The source supports the proposition that automating tasks or eliminating a particular job category does not by itself determine net employment outcomes. Its historical telephone-operator case treats replacement work as unresolved and finds no detectable wage or employment-share spillovers in the specific substitute occupations examined. This reinforces the synthesis’s caution against reading technical exposure or direct displacement as a forecast of economy-wide job loss. Material variation lies in scope: the study does not establish how generative AI will reshape particular tasks, firms or occupations, and its no-spillover finding is explicitly bounded rather than general. It also raises possible community, social-capital and intergenerational effects, but presents these as questions for further research rather than evidence against employment resilience. Because the source accepts the proposition’s core without materially extending its task-level framework, Supports is more appropriate than Builds on.

qs.q: As a result, questions such as whether, when, and how new work will materialize to offset the jobs lost to automation are not fully resolved.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: However, we do not see evidence of spillovers: wages did not fall in substitute occupations, and young white women’s share of these jobs did not grow.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The 2025 sources collectively accept the cluster’s principal proposition that task exposure does not mechanically imply occupational disappearance and materially develop its account of how task-level change produces uneven labour-market outcomes. Their common reasoning is that outcomes depend on heterogeneity below the occupational level—workers can reallocate effort across differently affected tasks, effects can be redistributed within firms and between employers while remaining muted in aggregate data, and the consequences depend on whether automation removes expert or supporting tasks rather than simply on how many tasks are exposed. Material internal variation concerns both mechanism and evidential strength. Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market provides a task-allocation model and empirical employment-share estimates, attributing variation to within-firm reallocation and differences across employers. The seniority-biased GenAI excerpt extends the analysis to junior versus senior workers and cites contrasting firm-level and aggregate findings, but frames junior displacement as a research question and supplies no results establishing it. Expertise adds a distinct scarcity-of-skills mechanism affecting wages, qualified labour supply and employment, but its evidence concerns the computerisation era and is explicitly illustrative rather than definitive for AI. These are complementary extensions, not a settled forecast of occupational or junior-worker decline, and the curated sources should not be treated as representative of all 2025 research.

qs.q: Comparing predicted to realized changes, we estimate that about 14% of the variation in occupational employment share growth can be attributed to their AI exposure during our sample period—roughly half from within-firm reallocation away from exposed tasks, and half from differences in average AI use across occupations’ employers.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Nevertheless, our expertise framework suggests a complementary but distinct conceptual focus for analyzing the relationship between automation and the value of labor: it is not merely                                                   52 ^Lthe quantity of tasks performed by an occupation or demographic group that determines demand for its labor, but also the scarcity of the expertise required to perform those tasks.
qs.a: Expertise · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The substantive 2026 source accepts the proposition that task exposure should not be equated with occupational disappearance and materially extends it by challenging fixed task bundles. It argues that changed activity costs can lead firms either to divide jobs into narrower specialist roles or recombine activities into broader generalist roles, thereby changing both occupational boundaries and the skills rewarded. This strengthens the cluster’s emphasis on job redesign and redistribution rather than direct inference from exposure to job loss. Its historical support is qualified: changes become visible only after entering job advertisements, titles or employment patterns, so observed classifications may lag emerging redesign. Internal variation in this curated pair arises from evidentiary availability rather than substantive disagreement: the other record is bibliography-only and therefore cannot be positioned.
